10. Single Sign-on Digital Identifier Platform. The facility for digital identification of users constitutes the backbone for the provision of e-government services as they allow safe, secure and legally verifiable access to these services. This facility creates the legal foundations for the validation of contractual and non-contractual interactions between the government and citizens. Digital identification allows governments to move services online, resulting in improvements in efficiency, productivity, and user satisfaction. In a post-disaster situation, this facility is critical to facilitate the transactions to which citizens typically need access (e.g. social transfers and citizen records such as deeds and birth certificates). Grenada currently has multiple and disparate systems for identification verification that impede ease of interaction with the government. The objective of this activity is to enable GOG to consolidate the different citizen identity systems that it currently employs into a unique, cloud-based digital identifier platform, which, together with the electronic payment system, will facilitate the provision of e-services that require authentication and authorization.

5. FSM has made substantial progress over the past decade to rollout new infrastructure and create the market conditions necessary to support investments in digital services. The passage of the Telecommunications Act of 2014 liberalized the telecommunications sector and removed the monopoly conferred on FSM Telecommunications Corporation (FSMTC) as the state-owned incumbent operator. The law also provided for the creation of the FSM Open Access Entity (OAE), also known as FSM Telecommunications Cable Corporation (FSMTCC), as a wholesale- only provider of backbone services. In addition, the law established the Telecommunication Regulation Authority (TRA) as the independent sector regulator. In terms of broadband infrastructure, with the support of the United States Rural Utilities Service (RUS), Pohnpei was connected via the HANTRU-1 submarine cable system in 2010. With the support of the ongoing World Bank FSM Connectivity Project (P130592), submarine cable systems now connect Yap (since mid-2018) and Chuuk (mid-2019). Work is also significantly advanced to connect Kosrae to the East Micronesia Cable (EMC) system, which is expected to enter service by mid-2021. The EMC system is a collaboration between FSM, Kiribati (financed by IDA) and Nauru (financed by the Asian Development Bank). FSM's IDA-financed submarine cable systems are owned and operated by the OAE. Access to capacity on the submarine cable systems is guaranteed on transparent, non-discriminatory and cost-based terms.

47. The blend of underground and aerial infrastructure for terrestrial fiber optic infrastructure will be determined during the final technical design and specification of the bidding documents. Aerial infrastructure capital expenditures (CAPEX) costs are almost two times lower and OPEX costs are slightly lower compared to underground infrastructure. However, aerial infrastructure is more vulnerable to natural disasters. Natural disasters such as typhoons occur regularly in FSM. With 8,400 mm of precipitation per year, Pohnpei is also one of the wettest regions in the world. This climate can damage an aerial network. If a disaster happens, aerial infrastructure may be damaged leading to outages and significant replacement costs. However, underground infrastructure faces other risks as well. Uncontrolled digging can damage the cables while people will be careful to stay away from the aerial cables since they would be adjacent to the power lines. Repair of underground infrastructure is more costly and more time- consuming. Flooding is also a particular threat to underground fiber infrastructure. It is assumed that the core fiber on each of the main islands (Pohnpei, Yap and Kosrae) will be buried underground. The periphery of the networks, including drops to individual premises, will be aerial utilizing existing infrastructure, particularly existing poles for electricity distribution. The cost of the fiber drops to individual premises is a relatively small proportion of total costs, comprising approximately US$1.1M of the US$8.8M total needed to install the on-island fiber infrastructure.

48. The deployment of the terrestrial fiber networks will also make possible the rollout of LTE networks on a cost- efficient basis. The installation of the LTE networks 14 will be done by competing mobile operators. Existing towers can be shared and most of the new cell sites can be very simple pole/small mast type of sites. There is no need for the new deployment of costly large towers. Adding more small and simple cell sites using fiber optic fronthaul capacity supplied by the OAE is more efficient—and utilizing the wholesale only OAE network on an open access and non-discriminatory and cost basis reduces the problems commonly associated with regulating access to essential facility infrastructure owned and controlled by vertically integrated operators. Each operator will establish and maintain a mobile core network, which may be located either within FSM or elsewhere in the region to improve utilization and economies of scale. On each island a local LTE radio access network (RAN) will be required for access to end-user mobile services. The estimated cost of each LTE RAN is approximately US$1.9 million for all 4 States, which assumes operators use existing towers, small fill-in sites and an existing mobile core network.

12. The primary technology for the network, given the capacity requirements to deliver the targets of the NBDS, will be OFC infrastructure. In the coming years, newer technologies (especially 5G wireless networks) might emerge as options, but currently they do not offer the same balance of quality and reliability as OFC networks.94 Where the costs of underground OFC deployment might prove to be prohibitive (e.g., in high-mountainous regions), or where cost savings are possible by using existing utility or public infrastructure, the network can be deployed using poles (e.g., for street lighting or electricity) and aerial cable.95 The costs of these deployments are lower, but they are more susceptible to some natural disasters such as landslides that are more likely in some regions. On the other hand, underground fiber networks are susceptible to flooding. Hence, in both cases, the design of the network shall seek to enhance climate resilience given the specific location. The precise mix of underground and aerial infrastructure for the network will be determined during the final technical design and reflected in the specifications of the bidding documents; at this time, the Project assumes about a third of the network will be aerial.

32. The expected growth in the digital economy will require robust government data infrastructure. The Government has adopted a government-wide approach to data infrastructure and is consolidating all government server rooms and Network Operations Centers (NOCs) into a standardized government cloud infrastructure. It is projected that this investment will support the growth of government ICT business operations over the next 5 to 10 years. Therefore, enhancing the data center infrastructure by acquiring storage, networking equipment, and computing resources for the government shared platform will enable cost-effective sharing of resources, increase reliability and security of electronic services offered by the government, enhance storage of government data, as well as create efficiency in sharing and accessing government applications through the shared infrastructure. As opposed to operating multiple siloed systems, resource sharing among government entities will also help reduce energy consumption. Besides this efficiency gain, considerations related to data center energy efficiency will be considered when expanding data center capacity (for example, use of renewables). In addition, when expanding data center infrastructure, climate risks will be taken into consideration, including robustness, back-up strategies, discontinuity plans, and training of staff on these.

7. International fiber optic connectivity. Congo is currently connected to only one submarine cable (West Africa Cable System (WACS16), with a landing station in Pointe-Noire, exclusively managed by the state- owned incumbent operator Congo Telecom (CT). Due to the current instable international connectivity (several outages occurred in 2020 and amid the presidential election in March 2021) and increased demand, there is an urgent need for diversification. Redundancy via terrestrial fiber optic links (currently owned by the GoC) remains limited. CT has an interconnection with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) since 2017 (10GB-capacity linking Brazzaville to Kinshasa through a sub-river cable) and Liquid Telecom, a leading private telecommunication operator in Africa, inaugurated a 20GB-capacity wireless link across the Congo River between Congo and DRC in September 2021. The interconnection with Gabon established under the World Bank-financed Central African Backbone (CAB) regional project (P122398) is operated and commercialized by Mambs Services (a Congolese private sector company) under a seven-year contract. Under the CAB Project, financed by the African Development Bank (AfDB), Congo should also interconnect with Cameroon and the Central African Republic. Due to COVID-19, the project has faced delays and is now expected to be completed by the end of 2022. Additionally, Meta-backed (previously Facebook) submarine cable project, 2Africa, plans to install a submarine cable landing station in Pointe-Noire by the end of 2022. The arrival of the new landing station cable is expected to help reduce prices and contribute to strong growth in broadband subscription.

Mauritania's geographic position, combined with its terrestrial fiber backbone (approximately 1,700 km deployed under WARCIP, with plans for 2,300 km more under WARDIP), creates strong potential for the country to become a transit hub for landlocked neighbors such as Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso. It is therefore a significant investment that will likely generate sizeable positive effects on broadband markets. 40. Under WARDIP SOP-1 and SOP-2, the participating countries—The Gambia, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, and Sierra Leone—have already undertaken substantial preparatory efforts to advance the development of a new West African submarine cable system aimed at strengthening international connectivity, improving resilience, and reducing dependence on single existing cable routes. These efforts have included the signing of a regional cooperation framework among the participating governments, the completion of extensive technical, financial, and commercial feasibility assessments, and a comprehensive market sounding process led with specialized transaction advisors. The market assessment reviewed multiple strategic options for connecting the countries to new international capacities, including standalone systems, connections to recently deployed cables, and integration into a broader new regional platform. The results of this analysis identified a connection to a new submarine cable project with wider regional reach, stronger resilience, and long-term scalability as the most viable option. Two suitable promoters were identified, and a competitive procurement has now advanced significantly, with bidding documents issued in March 2026 to the identified firms and contract award expected in July 2026. In terms of time and cost effectiveness, contracting with the cable system selected through the WARDIP competitive process represents a more efficient option for Mauritania than an independent procurement pursued at a later stage, while maximizing regional connectivity benefits.
